title: X.L.O. Concrete Corp. v. Rivergate Corp.
summary: A contract connected with an antitrust conspiracy was not automatically unenforceable; the court required a developed record on whether payment would enforce the prohibited arrangement itself.
notes: One introductory bracket in the edited excerpt appears inconsistent about the appellant. The fuller procedural account later in the same excerpt identifies dismissal, reinstatement; affirmance of the reinstatement order.

sections.Parties: X.L.O., a concrete subcontractor, sought the unpaid balance from Rivergate, the general contractor on a Manhattan construction project. Rivergate asserted an antitrust illegality defense under New York’s Donnelly Act.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties made a 1983 agreement for the project’s concrete superstructure and fills. X.L.O. completed the work and claimed $844,125.07 remaining due. The project had been allocated through the “Club,” an arrangement involving organized-crime leaders, concrete contractors, and a construction-workers’ union. The arrangement assigned large jobs, manipulated bids, and exacted a two-percent payment for labor peace. X.L.O. also gave a representative a $50,000 payment described as a gift. The negotiated contract price exceeded $16 million.

The record indicated that Rivergate knew of the Club and its rules. Thus the court faced both a serious scheme restraining competition and a contractor that had already furnished valuable work to a knowledgeable recipient.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court dismissed the complaint and certain counterclaims. The Appellate Division reinstated the complaint. The New York Court of Appeals affirmed that order, leaving factual issues for trial rather than finally awarding the contract balance.
sections.Issue: Did the contract’s connection to the Club require nonenforcement as a matter of law, or was a more specific inquiry into the claim and the unlawful restraint necessary?
sections.Holding: The antitrust defense did not defeat the claim automatically. Further evidence was needed to determine whether enforcing the agreement would compel the precise conduct prohibited by the antitrust law.
sections.Reasoning:
Courts are cautious about allowing a party to receive work and then avoid payment through an antitrust defense. A facially lawful contract does not become void solely because it resulted from a conspiracy. At the same time, a court must not become an instrument for enforcing the unlawful restraint itself.

Relevant questions included whether the agreement was an indivisible component of the scheme, whether the price was inflated or discriminatory because competition had been suppressed, and whether a judgment would complete the prohibited arrangement. The parties’ knowledge, relative culpability, and bargaining power also mattered. The court considered the possible forfeiture to the performing party, unjust enrichment of the recipient, and the potential availability of recovery for reasonable value. Direct public enforcement and statutory remedies reduced—but did not eliminate—the need to use nonenforcement as a deterrent. These considerations required development of the record, not a categorical conclusion that the conspiracy was harmless or that the contractor necessarily deserved payment.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Compare Blossom Farm to see why “connected to illegality” is an insufficient rule. The relationship between the specific performance sought, the prohibited conduct, and the parties’ relative positions must be explained.

topics.public-policy: The court asks whether enforcement would itself carry out the antitrust restraint.
topics.restitution: Forfeiture and unjust enrichment are relevant to the consequences of denying the contract claim.
topics.governing-law: Existing antitrust remedies and statutory policy inform the contract-enforcement analysis.

mnemonic.rationale: Concrete work on an illegal deal
